articles.title: How housing affordability can be achieved at the state and local level
articles.summary: Former Sen. Jon Tester praised the passage of the bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act, noting its success in balancing restrictions on Wall Street investors with incentives for professional housing providers to increase supply.
articles.body:
There’s one word on everyone’s mind in 2026: affordability. And when speaking about affordability, it’s hard not to mention housing. More than eight in 10 Americans say housing affordability is a problem where they live.

I’ve seen this at home in Montana. Since the pandemic, prices have jumped more than 66 percent, pushing homeownership even further out of reach for many working families. This isn’t just happening in Montana. In urban, suburban and rural communities across the country, families are unable to compete for housing. It should not be this difficult to find an affordable place to live.

Federal lawmakers made significant strides to reverse this trend, passing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act , a bipartisan housing package aimed at expanding supply, modernizing federal housing programs, and addressing the frustration families feel across the country. The law is not perfect, but it’s a positive step in the right direction.

Notably, the law caps the number of single-family homes that Wall Street landlords can purchase without impacting professional housing providers. Families looking for a home should not be pushed aside by Wall Street.

One of the intriguing features of the final bill is that it threaded the policy needle by capping Wall Street purchases, while ensuring that professional housing providers could still invest in refurbishing existing homes and building new homes to rent, thereby increasing supply and lowering home prices.

A previous version of the bill would have prevented investment in building new single-family homes for rent. Housing researchers and policy experts warned that this approach could chill construction, reduce rental options, and undermine the broader goal of increasing supply. The Urban Institute warned that the provision could reduce the number of rental units built each year by at least 72,000, while Pew urged lawmakers to revisit the government-mandate, which it said risked reducing much-needed rental housing.

During my time on the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, I saw firsthand how well-intentioned policies can create unintended barriers to housing development. When the goal is to make housing more affordable, policymakers should be looking for ways to remove barriers to supply, not create new requirements that make it harder and more expensive to build homes.

Approximately 34 percent of Americans rent . That number is 30 percent in Montana, where families young and old are looking for affordable housing options.

Policies that discourage rental housing would not only affect professional housing providers. They would also affect families in Billings, workers relocating for energy jobs, and seniors seeking flexibility. That is why Congress ultimately struck a more sensible balance and preserved the pieces that many of us — from Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) — supported.

But the work is not done. At the local and state level, zoning and permitting reforms are essential to build enough homes to keep up with population growth. Additionally, states and localities need to further enhance private investment in housing refurbishment and development — not only to increase supply, but also for reasons that may be less obvious to Montanans.

Private investment largely relies on pension funds. These funds invest in housing and generate returns that are used to pay pensioners regularly once they retire. Enabling private investment in housing ensures that we are taking care of Montana’s essential workers.

The Montana Teachers’ Retirement System and the Public Employees’ Retirement System manage billions of dollars in retirement funds for Montana teachers and public-sector workers, respectively. Montana also has pension funds for police officers and firefighters . Private investment in housing is a win-win situation.

More investment in home repairs and development creates more homes and helps maintain affordable housing prices for working families, while ensuring that Montana’s teachers, police and firefighters receive their fully-funded pensions and a comfortable retirement.

Expanding opportunity means expanding the number and types of homes available, not narrowing them. It means protecting renters as well as aspiring homeowners, while holding bad actors accountable without cutting off capital needed to build, repair and preserve housing.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act is a rare example of Congress listening, adjusting, and landing on a better policy. It took time and forced heated debates, but that is how legislating should work. It recognizes that slogans or scapegoats will not solve affordability.

It will be solved by building more homes, renovating the homes we already have, protecting consumers, and ensuring public policy encourages supply rather than discouraging it. Congress got that balance right. States should build on it, not undermine it.

Jon Tester, a Democrat, represented Montana in the U.S. Senate from 2007 to 2025.

articles.title: As oil edges higher, Trump floats letting Iran 'wither,' possibility of protracted war grows
articles.summary: President Trump, for the second day in a row, telegraphed an escalation in Iran after the midterm elections and an extended standoff, with the Strait of Horm...
articles.body:
President Trump, for the second day in a row, telegraphed an escalation in Iran after the midterm elections and an extended standoff, with the Strait of Hormuz still at the center of the conflict.

"The question is: Do we want to finish it off or do we just want to let it wither because we're getting everything we wanted," the president told reporters on Friday morning as he touted evidence of Middle East oil exports surpassing prewar levels.

The comments also came after Trump's ambassador to the UN told the Financial Times that the war could last another year and that the US is prepared for a long-term standoff, but that he hoped negotiations would end the conflict sooner.

US Ambassador Mike Waltz told the outlet that the US "can maintain [its] blockade for the foreseeable future."

The Trump administration will push for negotiations to end things more quickly, Waltz said, and he hoped the Iranians would "come to the table in a meaningful way before that." Major nuclear concessions, he said, are needed for peace.

Meanwhile, Trump on Thursday seemed to confirm reports that a new wave of strikes could be planned for after the election, saying, "We've knocked the hell out of them and we may do it a little bit further."

There is also growing evidence that the US Navy has helped ease some oil supply pressures.

A story from the Wall Street Journal based on data from shipping tracker Kpler — which Trump has touted repeatedly in recent days — found that Persian Gulf oil exports have now surpassed prewar levels through a combination of shipping routes and alternatives across the region, such as pipelines.

But the story also noted that oil traders are concerned the latest uptick might not be sustainable if fighting breaks out again.

Yet new fighting is what Trump has suggested for multiple days.

"We could, if we wanted to, just take all of the oil. We could take the whole country," he said Friday, claiming the Strait of Hormuz is "totally ours."

"We have done a hell of a job," the president said of the US Navy's blockade that has protected many oil exports, in spite of Iranian attacks, and also appears to have prevented Iran from exporting its own oil.

Global crude oil prices, meanwhile, remained elevated Friday, with futures for international benchmark Brent crude ( BZ=F ) above $110 per barrel and for US benchmark West Texas Intermediate ( CL=F ) above $100.

Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: 'A cyclical downturn is inevitable' in an AI crash: Strategist Dario Perkins
articles.summary: A new paper from TS Lombard strategist Dario Perkins games out how ugly things could get if the tech rout keeps gaining steam.
articles.body:
If the weakness in tech stocks continues to gain steam , it could end up being really ugly for investors, given how aggressively they have gone into tech stocks in recent years.

That's the warning in a new paper making the rounds on Friday from TS Lombard strategist Dario Perkins titled "Wargaming the AI Crash."

"The reality, of course, is that it is hard to identify the exact trigger for an AI crash. But we can model the fallout. In terms of financial markets, the impact is likely to be sizable. US stocks would be hit hard, with (at least) a 30% decline. That would wipe out around $20 trillion in market cap," Perkins said. Across debt markets and private credits, he estimated "$125–200 billion in losses. Spreads would blow out, and we should expect a wave of tech-related defaults."

"The weakest players in the AI ecosystem — the neoclouds , Oracle, standalone model developers and construction/equipment suppliers — would face acute distress," he added. "The hyperscalers would suffer serious revenue downgrades; and even the promise of lower capital spending (the return of free cash flow) would offer scant consolation. The traditional banking sector would not be immune."

In terms of how this would affect the US economy on a broader level, Perkins said, "A cyclical downturn is inevitable. Capital spending would plunge and confidence evaporate. There would be sizeable job losses in the construction sector. But as far as recessions go, we don't think this one would be particularly severe (at the milder end of historical norms). Not only is the macro footprint of the AI boom smaller than people think, but there is plenty of room for the Fed to cut rates. Ultimately, this policy response would be successful, especially for the bottom of America's K-shaped economy."

The backdrop for tech stocks has become increasingly fraught as October has played out.

Concerns began earlier this month with neocloud company CoreWeave ( CRWV ).

The company's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. That has triggered a subsequent sharp sell-off in the stock.

CoreWeave stock has been crushed in October to the tune of 35%.

Meta ( META ) then dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results this week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012 amid aggressive spending on AI.

The company said it would issue a new tranche of stock to help fuel its AI build-out.

Tesla ( TSLA ) also slashed its capital expenditures plan for the year by $5 billion to $20 billion.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Business confidence in India improved in the July-September quarter of FY2026-27 after declining for four consecutive quarters amid prolonged
articles.body: New Delhi: Business confidence in India improved in the July-September quarter of FY2026-27 after declining for four consecutive quarters amid prolonged geopolitical tensions, with expectations of higher production, domestic sales and exports lifting sentiment ahead of the festive season, according to a survey by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).The Business Confidence Index (BCI) rose to 107.8 in the second quarter from 99.8 in the preceding quarter, the latest NCAER Business Expectations Survey showed. However, the index remained significantly below the 142.6 recorded in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year.Conducted in September, the survey covered 502 firms of varying sizes across six cities — Delhi-NCR, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai and Pune.The improvement was broad-based, with the share of firms expecting economic conditions to improve over the next six months rising to 50% from 43% in Q1. Similarly, the proportion expecting their financial position to improve increased to 41% from 37%, while firms viewing the investment climate positively rose to 30% from 26%.Capacity utilisation sentiments also strengthened, with 94% of firms expecting utilisation to remain close to or above optimal levels, compared with 91% in the previous quarter.Confidence improved among both micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and large firms. The BCI for MSMEs increased to 100 from 93, while that for large firms rose to 120.3 from 111.6.“The data indicate a broad-based recovery in sentiments across both MSMEs and large firms,” said NCAER professor Bornali Bhandari, who led the survey.Growth expectations strengthened across key business indicators. articles.title: US consumer sentiment hits a near-record low before midterm elections
articles.summary: Independent voters’ economic anxieties highlight political implications of plummeting US consumer sentiment.
articles.body:
Consumer sentiment in the United States hit a near-record low in the final reading before the consequential midterm elections as cost-of-living issues weigh on US consumers.

The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers said its Consumer Sentiment Index dropped on Friday as continuing tensions between the US and Iran drove up prices at the grocery store and the petrol pump.

The reading dropped to 48.0 this month from a final reading of 48.1 in September, leading to the second-lowest reading on record. The lowest was only a few months ago in May, when it stood at 44.8 points.

The report measures how consumers feel about their personal finances at present and how they expect it will change over the next 12 months; whether they feel it is a good time to make major household purchases; and their expectations for the US economy over the next 12 months, as well as five years.

“Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers. “Sentiment is now 10 percent below a year ago and 15 percent less than February, just prior to the Iran conflict.”

Crucially, weaker sentiment was fuelled by self-identified political independents. The group’s sentiment dropped to 42.4 points, slightly above the all-time low of 40.6 points, which it reached in May.

Since January, the number of independents pointing to inflation pressures hurting their financial situation rose by 27 percent. Republicans referencing the same issue rose by 52 percent, and the figure rose by 15 percent among Democrats.

Households with no or limited exposure to the stock market — which until recently had been soaring on enthusiasm for the artificial intelligence investment boom — have also cited high prices as a drag on their finances more frequently than at the start of the year.

Consumers’ expectations for inflation over the next five years rose to 3.5 percent from 3.4 percent in September and 3.2 percent in March.

“Consumers broadly expect inflation to accelerate, and this year’s increases in inflation expectations are not limited to one part of the political spectrum,” Hsu wrote. “The fact that aggregate consumer spending has been relatively resilient despite negative views of the economy provides another reason for caution. If part of consumption currently reflects precautionary spending to avoid future price hikes, disinflation may be even more difficult to achieve.”

The sentiment comes amid heightened prices for consumers . Inflation rose by 3.7 percent year on year last week, according to the recent consumer price index report, and petrol prices remain high, although lower than a month ago.

The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.29 ($1.13 per litre) on Friday, down from $4.47 ($1.18 per litre) this time last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices.

Friday’s report comes in advance of the final monetary policy decision before the midterm elections. On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve is largely expected to maintain rates at 3.75–4.00 percent after raising rates by 25 basis points in September. CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of certain monetary policy decisions, forecasts an 89.5 percent chance that rates will remain unchanged.

articles.title: Consumers across party lines are fed up with high gas prices
articles.summary: High gas prices and years of persistently elevated inflation continue to drag down US consumer sentiment to historically low levels, new data showed Friday.
articles.body: A gallon of unleaded gas costs 40% more today than it did last year. A gallon of diesel is running nearly 75% higher. As for Americans’ optimism about the economy 11 days before the midterm elections? That’s nearly running on empty. High gas prices and years of persistently elevated inflation continue to drag down US consumer sentiment to historically low levels, new data showed Friday. The University of Michigan’s October consumer sentiment index was the second lowest on records that go back to 1978. The record low of 44.8 was set in May, a month that saw the national average for a gallon of unleaded hit a four-year high of $4.56 because of oil supply shocks stemming from the war with Iran. Five months later, those weekly trips to the gas pumps aren’t feeling much better: And there’s not a lot of optimism those numbers will improve. “There is broad consensus that escalation is coming and that it could diminish flows of oil out of the Middle East,” said Gregory Brew, senior analyst at consulting firm Eurasia Group. “Right now, a lot of oil is coming out, but it’s expensive,” he added. “There is very little confidence that supply is sustainable.” Price pain across party lines Consumer sentiment is now 10% below where it was last year and 15% down from February, before the war began, according to Friday’s report. Consumers are frustrated that their purchasing power has declined while prices continue to climb higher, said Joanne Hsu, University of Michigan economist and director of the Surveys of Consumers. In October, 56% of surveyed consumers spontaneously mentioned that higher prices are negatively affecting their personal finances, Hsu said. That share has increased for four months in a row. “These increases are seen across the political spectrum, with Republicans exhibiting the largest proportional rise,” Hsu said in a statement. “Similarly, consumers with no stock holdings or very small holdings also report increased concerns over the effect of high prices on their personal finances over the course of the year.” Consumers with the largest stock holdings, however, reported little change in the burden of high prices since February, she added. And the recent hike in interest rates is starting to play a factor as well, she said, noting homebuying conditions “plummeted,” with 85% of surveyed consumers saying it’s a bad time to buy a home. The latest survey also showed that consumers expect inflation to remain high in the months and years to come. Year-ahead inflation expectations ticked up to 4.7% from 4.6% and moving even further from the 3.4% seen in February before the US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Long-run expectations moved higher to 3.5% from 3.4%. Consumers’ expectations about the pace of future price hikes are closely tracked by the Federal Reserve. If people believe that prices will only continue to rise, they might spend more now and demand higher wages, and businesses might raise prices to accommodate higher demand and wages – thus raising inflation. The Fed’s rate-setting committee meets next week, with a decision expected Wednesday at 2 p.m. ET., its last move on borrowing costs before the midterms.

articles.title: Exclusive-First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
articles.summary: Oct 23 () - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker...
articles.body:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on ‌Friday.

Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of ‌November 3 US midterm elections.

Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless ​countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.

The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.

The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be ‌the first imported by the US since former ⁠President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.

Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, ⁠to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.

"As far ​as I'm ​aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy ​that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail ‌for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.

The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.

RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTSSince the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.

Shipping data from ‌LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages ​to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at ​least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.

It ​was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic ‌Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.

Russian Deputy ​Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said ​additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.

articles.title: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500 drop, Nasdaq rises after sharp tech sell-off
articles.summary: Stocks were headed lower on Friday to cap a volatile week.
articles.body: US stocks were mixed on Friday as worries over the AI trade lingered, following this week's steep sell-off in Tech (XLK) that triggered a flight to bonds. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 1.2%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) dropped 0.4%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) steadied close to the flatline after semiconductors and Big Tech sold off on Thursday.The 10-year Treasury (^TNX) yield held below the 5% threshold as investors flocked to bonds. The AI trade attempted a rebound following concerns over rising financing costs and a potential slowdown in capex, which weighed on already-battered neocloud stocks like CoreWeave (CRWV). Shares of AI chip giants Nvidia (NVDA) and AMD (AMD) edged higher, along with other infrastructure plays, after Thursday's sell-off.Shares of this week's earnings headliners, SpaceX (SPCX), Tesla (TSLA), and Meta (META), stabilized in Friday trading after declining in the previous session.Not all of tech was struggling on Friday, though. Cybersecurity stocks, including SailPoint (SAIL), Cloudflare (NET), and Palo Alto Networks (PANW), each rose more than 5%. Oil prices remained near a five-month high amid fears of escalating tensions in the Middle East, with Brent crude (BZ=F) hovering near $112 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate crude (CL=F) climbing to $103 per barrel.
